_about: A theme's front page (plan 7.6b; Doug, 2026-10-06: 'a one stop entry point to understanding what the Bible really says about this topic ... on its own terms'; 'a theme cannot be expected to hold it all on one page - it is an entry point for many other pages'). Its opening in plain words and the texts' own, the page it hinges on as its first door, a place to begin for a reader new to it, its other doors, and its note. Every quotation machine-checked against the Berean (tests/test_readings_text.py). `imagery`: the table the page hinges on -- its file, its door's words (also its page's title), its address under the theme (`slug`), and short column names for the index.

apocalyptic.intro: Passages in which someone is shown what is hidden, in visions: thrones, beasts, scrolls, a city, a river. Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah and Revelation are full of them, and many of the same images appear in more than one book.
opening: the heavens opened and I saw visions of God

I looked out into the night and saw a man riding on a red horse
This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants
apocalyptic.note: These pages set side by side what the texts themselves say. They take no interpretive stance: they do not say what any image stands for, whom it refers to, whether one passage looks forward to another, or when anything happens. Readers and traditions (preterist, historicist, futurist, idealist, and others) read these passages differently, and every reading can start from the same words.

imagery.blurb: images set out across Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, the other prophets, the Gospels and letters, and Revelation, each in the passages' own words, with what is alike and what differs.

starters: The throne and the living creatures

apocalyptic.starters_hint: You do not need to take in all of it. Pick one image and read what each book says about it.

law_wisdom.intro: The Law, in two parts. First, where it was set out: “the law that Moses set before the Israelites” (Deuteronomy 4:44), its commandments, and the places that quote them. Second, where the New Testament speaks of it, opening at Matthew 5:17: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17); “love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10). Set first here are the two commandments of which Jesus says “No other commandment is greater than these” (Mark 12:31): “Love the Lord your God” and “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37-39; Mark 12:30-31). And the page meets Wisdom at Ecclesiastes 12:13: “Fear God and keep His commandments”.

freedom.intro: Freedom in the texts' own words: “Do not be afraid”, “Be anxious for nothing”, “will not be put to shame”; slaves to sin, and set free; “no longer a slave, but a son”; the yoke broken and the yoke offered; liberty proclaimed; and “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free.”
opening: where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom
Do not fear, for I am with you
Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you
the truth will set you free
to proclaim liberty to the captives
It is for freedom that Christ has set us free
freedom.note: These pages set side by side what the texts themselves say. They take no stance where readers and traditions differ: freedom from the Law, free will, and whether the freedom spoken of is political or inward. Every reading can start from the same words.

imagery.blurb: wordings of fear and its end, of anxiety, of shame, and of bondage and release that more than one book shares, from the Exodus to the Gospels and the letters, with what is alike and what differs.

children_of_god.intro: God's children in the texts' own words: “that we should be called children of God”, the right to become children of God, sons of the living God, “Israel is My firstborn son”, born again, adoption, “Abba, Father”, heirs, and Jesus' brothers, each said to those its verse names.
opening: Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God
He gave the right to become children of God
The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God
children_of_god.note: These pages set side by side what the texts themselves say. They take no stance where readers and traditions differ: who God's children are, how Israel and the church relate, and whether “born of water and the Spirit” speaks of baptism. Every reading can start from the same words.
